# Introduction

The sampling distribution of a statistic is the distribution of that statistic
over all possible samples of a given size. It is the conceptual bridge between a
single observed sample and the population parameter we wish to estimate.

## Why it matters

- Underpins confidence intervals
- Underpins hypothesis testing
- Quantifies estimator variability

# Methods

We simulated $10\,000$ samples of size $n$ from a range of population
distributions and recorded the sample mean for each.

- Populations: uniform, exponential, bimodal
- Sample sizes: $n \in \{5, 30, 100\}$
- Outcome: distribution of $\bar{X}$

# Results

For all populations, the distribution of $\bar{X}$ approached normality as $n$
increased, with variance shrinking in proportion to $1/n$ — consistent with the
Central Limit Theorem.

::: {.callout-note}
Even strongly skewed populations yielded near-normal sample means by $n = 30$.
:::

# Conclusion

The Central Limit Theorem holds robustly across population shapes, justifying
normal-theory inference for moderately large samples.
